Thank you for asking me to review your patient in the Neurology Clinic today. He lives in supported accommodation where rotating staff maintain daily seizure charts, which we used as the primary source for today’s assessment.

Since his last review here in March 2025, the charts and his account suggest a fluctuating pattern with brief episodes most days. I have provided them with a simplified event documentation template and asked that they continue the daily charting and note any injuries, prolonged events (>5 minutes), or need for rescue medication. - Continue current anti-seizure regimen unchanged for now while we collect a further four weeks of structured logs from the supported accommodation team. 
- Arrange a routine EEG and repeat bloods (FBC, U&E, LFTs) to coincide with his next clinic visit.

Diagnosis: 

Generalised epilepsy with improved control on current regimen; prior valproate exposure discontinued 

Aetiology: 

Presumed genetic generalised epilepsy; no structural lesion identified on prior MRI; normal perinatal and developmental history 

Other Medical Problems: 

Intermittent mechanical low back pain related to manual handling at work; no red flags

Continue Lamotrigine 100 mg mane, 100 mg nocte, same brand. Maintain Levetiracetam 500 mg mane, 1,000 mg nocte. Reinforce adherence and maintain supply in weekly organiser. Dear Dr Ahmed,

Sophie Bennett, DOB: 12-03-1992, Hospital No: H583920 NHS No. 9081726345
Flat 3, Rosewood Assisted Living, 14 Brook Street, London, W1K 5DL

Medication:

Levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily. Patient-reported adherence is good, with no missed doses in the past month. No adverse effects beyond mild transient irritability in the evenings.

Background and supports:

The patient resides in assisted living and is supported by a key worker; key-worker notes were reviewed where available. These corroborate stable routines, medication prompts, and no safeguarding concerns.

Epilepsy history and current status:

This patient has focal epilepsy. Seizures have historically begun with a rising epigastric sensation and brief speech arrest, progressing on occasion to impaired awareness with right-hand automatisms; there have been no generalised tonic–clonic seizures reported in the past year. Last seizure on 31-May, described as a brief focal aware event lasting approximately 20–30 seconds without loss of awareness, occurring in the late afternoon after a disrupted sleep routine. No injuries. Since then, no further events have been recorded by the patient or noted by the key worker.

Triggers and lifestyle factors:

Patient reports poor sleep and higher work-related stress in late May around the time of the last event. Caffeine intake has been reduced since June and sleep hygiene improved with a consistent bedtime routine, which may have contributed to subsequent stability.

Investigations and monitoring:

Previous MRI (2019) unremarkable. Routine EEG (2020) showed left temporal intermittent rhythmic activity without definitive epileptiform discharges. No new investigations requested today in view of clinical stability. We have asked the key worker to continue logging any spells of altered awareness or behavioural arrest, and to document potential triggers.

Plan:

- Continue levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily unchanged.
- Maintain seizure diary (patient and key worker) with attention to sleep, stressors, and any focal aware symptoms.
- Safety advice reviewed; no driving. Occupational risk currently low within supervised environment.
- Consider repeat EEG only if events recur or evolve.

Follow-up:

We will review in six months, or sooner if there are further seizures or concerning changes.

Yours sincerely

Dear Dr A. Patel
Consultant Neurologist,  

Daniel Harris, DOB: 14-03-1989, Hospital No: KCH-782311 NHS No. 9432015876  
12 Brookside Close, London, SE15 3QT

Thank you for your referral. I reviewed Daniel Harris following concerns raised by his employer about recurrent collapse events occurring during shifts in a commercial kitchen. He works the hot line in a high-temperature, fast-paced environment, often during evening service. He attended today with his colleague who has witnessed several recent episodes.

According to the colleague, the typical event begins without warning while he is plating or working over the grill. He becomes unresponsive, stares ahead, and his posture slackens; there may be low, indistinct vocal sounds. On two occasions he slid down a stainless-steel unit and briefly rocked at the shoulders. There has been no clearly observed rhythmic limb jerking, tongue biting, or incontinence reported. He appears confused after the episode and needs 30–60 minutes before he can resume tasks, often describing a heavy head and overwhelming fatigue. He does not reliably recall the event itself.

Daniel Harris reports that these episodes crop up most shifts, especially during the busiest part of service, and his manager has had to reassign him from open flame stations as a precaution. He also notes that, on getting home, he sometimes wakes disoriented on the sofa with no memory of lying down, suggesting possible unwitnessed events outside work as well. Heat, noise, and pressure to keep pace may be contributory triggers from his perspective.

Medication history: he has recently restarted levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily after a lapse in adherence due to rota changes and missed GP appointments; he believes that when he takes treatment consistently, the kitchen events thin out to only the odd occurrence across a handful of shifts. He denies alcohol misuse; he drinks coffee during service and little fluid otherwise. Sleep is fragmented due to alternating late finishes and early prep starts.

Examination today was unremarkable. Neurological assessment between episodes showed normal cranial nerves, full strength, intact coordination, and no focal deficits. Cardiovascular observations were stable with no orthostatic drop. There were no features to suggest an active intercurrent illness. Collateral descriptions are limited by the hectic nature of the kitchen and the lack of continuous observation.

Given the ongoing events arising on most working days and the safety-critical environment (sharp tools, hot oil, open flames), further characterisation is necessary. I have requested urgent ambulatory EEG with concurrent event diary, and I will also arrange a sleep-deprived EEG if the first study is non-diagnostic. Basic bloods (FBC, U&E, LFT, bone profile, glucose, magnesium) and serum antiseizure medication level have been ordered. I have advised the employer and patient that a temporary restriction from high-risk stations is prudent pending assessment, and the patient will discuss adjusted duties with occupational health. We also talked about hydration and structured meal breaks during service, as he reports going long stretches without fluids.

Daniel Harris understands the plan and agrees to keep a detailed log of events, noting timing, context (heat level, task, stress), and recovery period. I will review him in clinic after investigations. Please let me know if there is any additional history from primary care that would assist, particularly previous imaging or prior EEG results.

Yours sincerely

Plan: Patient will maintain a detailed seizure and trigger log, including light exposure details. She will utilise blue-light reduction and regular rest breaks with screens as tolerated. Dear Dr Tomas 
Consultant Neurologist,  

Daniel Harris, DOB: 14-03-1986, Hospital No: K917204 NHS No. 7489203156  
Flat 12, Mariners Court, 8 Dockside Way, London, SE16 3AB

Thank you for asking me to review this gentleman. We conducted a planned telephone consultation while he was onshore between offshore rotations. He reports a longstanding history of generalised epilepsy. He may go four to five days without seizures, but when they happen he often has them in batches, with two - three occurring within 24 hours. He and his partner describe typical events as abrupt loss of awareness with generalised stiffening and rhythmic jerking lasting around 60–90 seconds, followed by post-ictal confusion for up to 30 minutes. He occasionally bites his tongue and has had one shoulder strain in the past but no recent injuries. There is no consistent focal onset aura reported.

He works offshore on a two-weeks-on, two-weeks-off rotation. Seizures tend to cluster either at the end of a run of night shifts or within the first 48 hours after returning onshore, which he attributes to sleep disruption and variable meal times. He denies alcohol excess and states he avoids caffeine late in the day. He uses a medication alarm and a written seizure log while offshore. Occupational Health have placed him on restricted duties when offshore; he confirms he does not undertake safety-critical tasks on days following a seizure.

He is currently taking valproate 1,000 mg twice daily and levetiracetam 1,500 mg twice daily with good adherence. No clear adverse effects are reported beyond mild irritability during periods of poor sleep. He has rescue buccal midazolam available but has not needed to use it in the last three months. He has not driven and understands DVLA regulations. He last had a generalised tonic–clonic seizure 10 days ago, with two events occurring the same day, and none since. 

Past EEGs (most recently last year) showed generalised spike-and-wave discharges consistent with a generalised epilepsy syndrome; prior MRI brain was normal. There is no family history of epilepsy known. He has had no recent infections, head injuries, or changes in prescribed medication.

Impression: Generalised epilepsy with clustering related to sleep disruption and rota transitions. Current regimen is broadly effective with intermittent breakthrough clusters as described above. We discussed optimising sleep hygiene during shift transitions and maintaining strict regularity of doses while offshore. He prefers to continue the present regimen for now. We agreed to continue telephone reviews when he is onshore, with the option of bringing him for a routine EEG update in the next 6–9 months if breakthrough clusters increase. He will contact the clinic sooner if he experiences prolonged seizures, increased frequency, or any injuries.

Plan:
- Continue valproate 1,000 mg twice daily and levetiracetam 1,500 mg twice daily.
- Maintain rescue midazolam for prolonged seizures (>5 minutes) and cluster management per prior plan.
- Reinforce sleep and shift-transition strategies; continue seizure diary.
- Occupational Health restrictions to remain unchanged offshore.
- Telephone review during his next onshore period in approximately 8–10 weeks, or earlier if seizures escalate.

Yours sincerely

I reviewed Sophie Williams in epilepsy clinic today. She has a learning disability and was accompanied by her paid carer, who assists with communication and maintains a seizure log. The carer provided the primary history, supplemented by brief responses from the patient.

She has focal epilepsy. Seizure semiology as described by the carer involves brief behavioural arrest with right upper limb clenching and head deviation to the right, sometimes progressing to impaired awareness with lip smacking; post-ictal confusion typically lasts 5–10 minutes. There have been no reported injuries. The carer noted both daytime and nocturnal events in prior months. She has had no seizures so far this month, four in August, one in July and 3 in June, with events reported from both daytime and nocturnal periods. Triggers suspected by the carer include sleep deprivation and missed meals; there has been added emphasis on consistent routines within the supported living setting.

No recent intercurrent illnesses. Sleep is reported as improved after adjusting evening support staff schedules. Appetite is stable. There have been no new neurological symptoms. The patient uses a pill organiser and carer-administered reminders; no missed doses were recorded on the log since early August.

Examination today: she was alert, engaged with prompts, and followed simple commands. Speech output limited but consistent with baseline. Cranial nerves grossly intact; no focal motor deficit appreciated. Gait steady with supervision. Observations stable.

Investigations: Prior MRI (2022) showed left mesial temporal sclerosis; routine EEG (2023) with left temporal sharp waves. No recent bloods indicating adverse effects; carer to arrange annual monitoring via primary care as per shared care plan.

Plan: 
- Continue levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily. 
- Reinforce adherence and sleep hygiene within the supported living plan; carer to continue detailed seizure logging, including time of day, semiology, duration, and recovery. 
- Provide a written, easy-read seizure first aid guide to the care team; we have updated her seizure management plan with contact numbers. 
- Consider lamotrigine adjunct if frequency increases or if clusters recur; at present, with no seizures recorded this month, we will not make a change. 
- Safety: nocturnal supervision maintained; no current driving. 

We will review her again in four months, or sooner if the seizure frequency increases or if there is any change in pattern such as prolonged events, new injuries, or generalised tonic–clonic activity.

Yours sincerely

Diagnosis: 

Generalised epilepsy with absence, myoclonic, and previously documented generalised tonic-clonic seizures. Good response to Valproate; Topiramate poorly tolerated due to cognitive side effects. 

Aetiology: 

Presumed genetic generalised epilepsy; normal MRI brain; prior routine EEG with generalised 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges. 

Other Medical Problems: 

History of migraine without aura; iron deficiency previously addressed with oral supplementation. High caffeine intake acknowledged (self-reported 5–6 strong coffees per day). 

Management Plan: 

Continue Sodium Valproate 500 mg mane and 1000 mg nocte. Reinforce adherence and single-brand prescribing. Arrange repeat trough valproate level, LFTs, FBC, and BMI check in three months. Provide written advice regarding sleep regularity and limiting caffeine, particularly late afternoon/evening, as she has noticed jitteriness and occasional palpitations on higher intake. DVLA guidance previously discussed and remains applicable. Review in six months or sooner if breakthrough generalised tonic-clonic seizures occur. 

Seizure activity is infrequent. She reports one absence seizure every one to two day and has been free of tonic-clonic seizures for over nine months. Occasional morning myoclonic jerks continue, though they are mild and do not interfere significantly with daily function. She links mild morning jerks and brief lapses in concentration to nights of shorter sleep and higher caffeine use; these episodes have not resulted in injuries or work absences. She remains in full-time employment and uses a smartphone diary to log events, which correlates with the above pattern. 

We reviewed lifestyle factors today. She acknowledges high caffeine consumption and is considering reducing this gradually. We agreed a neutral monitoring approach, with her continuing to record intake, sleep duration, and any seizure activity. No medication changes were made during this visit. 

Yours sincerely
